findings.title: Web: if any of the 12 fonts takes more than 12 s to load, the app shows a blank page forever
findings.detail: `const [fontsLoaded] = useFonts(FONT_FILES);` throws away the error value, and line 74 has `if (!fontsLoaded || !hydrated) return null;`. On web, expo-font loads each font through FontFaceObserver with a fixed 12 s timeout: node_modules/expo-font/build/ExpoFontLoader.web.js:130 `.load(resource.testString ?? null, 12000)`. That check runs on Chrome, Android Chrome and Firefox; `isFontLoadingListenerSupported` only skips it on Safari/iOS. loadAsync wraps all 12 fonts in one Promise.all (Font.js:71). useRuntimeFonts sets `loaded` only when that promise resolves; on rejection it sets `error` and never retries. FONT_FILES puts about 2.35 MB of TTF on the critical path: Andika_400Regular.ttf alone is 647 KB (x2), Nunito is 132 KB (x5) and Lexend is 78 KB (x5). Lexend is loaded even when the dyslexia font is off. All of it has to arrive within 12 s, which needs about 1.6 Mbit/s sustained. Example: a learner on a slow 3G connection opens the web app for the first time, one font times out, and RootLayout renders null for the rest of the page's life. There is no error screen and no retry.
findings.fix: Read the error: `const [fontsLoaded, fontError] = useFonts(...)` and render once `fontsLoaded || fontError`, since system fonts are an acceptable fallback. Better still, load only Nunito and Andika at boot and load Lexend lazily when dyslexiaFont is switched on. Consider subset/woff2 Andika files for the web build.

findings.title: Web: two open tabs overwrite each other's outbox index, so answers are orphaned (progress marks too)
findings.detail: Outbox caches its index in memory once per process: loadIndex returns `this.index` after the first read and never reads storage again. enqueue writes `next = [...ids, record.client_uuid]` built from that cached array (lines 139-148). On web, AsyncStorage is window.localStorage (async-storage lib/module/AsyncStorage.js:59-65), which every tab of the origin shares. Nothing listens for `storage` events or BroadcastChannel (grep finds no match in src). Each tab loads the index when it mounts, because the useBootstrap sync effect calls outbox.list(). Example: tab A and tab B are both signed in as the same learner (F8 makes each tab sign in separately). The learner finishes a 20-answer lesson in tab A, so the index holds idx0 plus 20 rows. Later they answer one item in tab B, which writes idx0 plus 1. Tab A's 20 row keys stay in localStorage but are no longer in the index. They are never listed, synced, counted in Settings or exported, yet they still use quota. The same last-writer-wins problem hits useLearner.update (src/state/learner.ts:72-77): it writes the whole LearnerData from its in-memory snapshot, so `completed` marks and saved words from the other tab are lost. Prefs persistence has the same issue.
findings.fix: Inside `serial()`, re-read the index from storage before every mutation, at least on web, or listen for `window.addEventListener('storage')` and invalidate `this.index`. A more robust option is to drop the separate index and enumerate rows by key prefix (getAllKeys), so no single key can drop rows. For learner data, re-read and merge per field (completed and savedWords are unions) before writing, or subscribe to `storage` events and reload.

findings.title: A failed outbox write drops the answer silently, and one failed index read breaks the outbox until restart
findings.detail: (1) `this.loading ??= this.store.getItem(...).then(...)` has no rejection handler that resets `this.loading`. If that first getItem rejects (localStorage SecurityError or quota error on web, an AsyncStorage/SQLite error on Android), `this.index` stays null and every later loadIndex() returns the same rejected promise. Every enqueue, list and acknowledge then fails for the rest of the process. (2) The caller treats a rejected enqueue as a log line only: LessonRunner.tsx:171 `.catch((e: unknown) => log.error('outbox.enqueue_failed', e))`, while setOutboxFull is set only when enqueue returns `false`. The learner gets correct/incorrect feedback and the lesson continues, but the answer was never stored. The outbox contract in its own header comment says rows are 'never dropped silently'. Realistic triggers: web localStorage quota (the cap of 5,000 rows at about 600 chars each is roughly 3M chars), private-mode storage, or Android's 6 MB AsyncStorage default (async-storage/android/config.gradle:90 `dbSizeInMB = 6L`). A related gap: useLearner.update does `void writeJson(...)` with no catch, so a failed progress write becomes an unhandled rejection and the in-memory state silently diverges from what is on disk.
findings.fix: In loadIndex, use `.catch(e => { this.loading = null; throw e; })`. Have the runner surface an enqueue rejection the same way it surfaces `false` (the outbox-full notice or a 'couldn't save this answer' notice), and keep the record in memory so it can be retried. Write the row and the index in one `multiSet`, which is atomic on native. Add a catch with log plus UI state to learner.update's write.

findings.title: Outbox sync is hard-wired to `null`: it will not start when the endpoint appears, and nothing triggers it after an answer
findings.detail: useBootstrap calls `syncOutbox(getOutbox(learnerId), null)` unconditionally. The `transportFor` named in sync.ts's header comment ('Until `npm run gen:api` picks them up, `transportFor` returns null') does not exist. `serverSupportsSync()` is referenced only by a unit test, and no SyncTransport implementation exists anywhere in src. DECISIONS §9.4 says 'Sync switches itself on when POST /v1/sync/reviews appears in the regenerated schema'. That is false: regenerating the API changes nothing, and answers keep accumulating up to OUTBOX_CAPACITY (5,000), after which new answers are refused. Even once a transport exists, the effect runs only when `[learnerId, network]` change. An answer given while online is not sent until the network flips or the app restarts, because there is no trigger on enqueue, on foreground or on a timer, and nothing guards against two syncs running at once.
findings.fix: Implement `transportFor(api): SyncTransport | null` that returns null unless `serverSupportsSync()`, and pass its result instead of `null`. Trigger a debounced sync on outbox emit, on AppState 'active' and on reconnect, behind a single-flight guard like the auth refresh.

findings.title: words/lexicon loaders keep a failed promise forever, so Retry can never succeed (web)
findings.detail: `this.words ??= this.source.read('words').then(...)` and `this.lexicon ??= this.source.read('lexicon').then(...)` (line 125) never clear the field on failure, unlike loadCourse, which does `.catch(e => { this.course = null; throw e; })`, and loadUnit, which deletes its cache entry. On web, source.app.ts reads these files with `fetch(asset.uri)` over the network (DECISIONS F26: on web, units load on demand). Example: a learner loads the app, loses the connection before words.lep or lexicon.lep is fetched, and the read rejects. TanStack's retry and the lesson route's Retry button (`void words.refetch()`) both call `content.loadWords()`, which returns the same rejected promise. The lesson screen (`error = course.error ?? words.error ?? ...`) and story tap-gloss stay broken after the connection returns, until a full page reload, which on web also signs the learner out (F8).
findings.fix: Mirror loadCourse: `this.words ??= this.source.read('words').then(...).catch((e) => { this.words = null; throw e; });`, and the same for lexicon.

findings.title: Offline app opens are not recorded, so reminders get cut to weekly for learners who did open the app
findings.detail: The upkeep effect returns early with `if (status !== 'signedIn' || minor === undefined) return;`, where `minor = me.data?.is_minor`. When the app starts offline (the core offline-lesson use case on native), /v1/me fails and `lastOpenedAt` is never updated. Nothing wires TanStack's onlineManager or focusManager to NetInfo or AppState (grep finds no `onlineManager|focusManager` in src). On React Native, `refetchOnReconnect` therefore never fires, and the always-mounted useBootstrap observer stays in its error state after the connection returns; only mounting Profile, Progress or Settings refetches /v1/me. reminderUpkeep then calls `missedSince(new Date(r.lastOpenedAt), now, ...)` against a stale lastOpenedAt. Example: the learner does lessons offline every day for five days. On the first foreground with /v1/me loaded, every reminder since the last online open counts as 'ignored', `weekly = true` is applied and reminders are downgraded, even though the learner opened the app daily. This breaks the documented rule that opening the app resets the count.
findings.fix: Record `lastOpenedAt` and reset `ignoredInARow` on every AppState 'active', independent of /v1/me. Run only the missed/weekly evaluation once `minor` is known, or use the more conservative minor schedule when it is unknown. Also wire `onlineManager.setEventListener` to NetInfo and `focusManager` to AppState so /v1/me refetches on reconnect and foreground.

findings.title: No timeout covers reading the response body, so a stalled refresh blocks every authenticated request
findings.detail: send() clears its abort timer in `finally` as soon as `cfg.fetch` resolves, which happens once headers arrive (line 77 returns `{ response, requestId }`, line 89 `clearTimeout(timer)`). The body is read afterwards with no deadline. In Session.doRefresh, `const tokens = (await response.json()) as TokenResponse;` (session.ts:214) runs inside the single-flight promise, and `this.refreshing` is cleared only in its `.finally`. If a flaky mobile connection stalls after the headers (common on poor networks; expo/fetch streams the body), that promise never settles. Every later `accessToken()` / `fetchAuthed()` returns the same pending promise, so /v1/me and all future authenticated calls hang until the app is killed. signIn and register have the same unguarded `response.json()`.
findings.fix: Keep the AbortController alive until the body has been consumed. For example, have send() take a `read` callback (json/text) and clear the timer after it, or wrap body reads in `Promise.race` with a timeout that calls `controller.abort()`. At least give doRefresh an overall deadline so `this.refreshing` is always cleared.

findings.title: outbox.list() reads every row with its own sequential getItem, on every reconnect and every Settings refresh, and nothing ever drains the outbox
findings.detail: `for (const id of ids) { const raw = await this.store.getItem(...) }` makes one native AsyncStorage call per row. list() runs from syncOutbox, which useBootstrap calls whenever `learnerId` or `network` changes, so on every NetInfo flap. Even with a null transport it lists all rows before returning 'waiting_for_server'. It also runs from useOutboxRows on every emit while Privacy settings is open, and from buildExport. Because sync is hard-wired off, the outbox only grows, up to 5,000 rows. On Android that means 5,000 serial bridge and SQLite reads per flap. Android AsyncStorage runs on a serial executor, so that queue sits ahead of the next enqueue's setItem and lengthens the window in which an app kill loses an answer. Each enqueue also rewrites the full index (about 195 KB at capacity).
findings.fix: Use `AsyncStorage.multiGet(keys)` (add `multiGet` to KeyValueStore). In syncOutbox, return 'waiting_for_server' before listing when transport is null. Settings only needs counts by status, which can be cached in the index metadata.

findings.title: Story tap-gloss shows the wrong word: 'hates' as 'hat', 'cares' as 'car'
findings.detail: lookup() tries the `-es` strip before the `-s` strip and returns the first candidate that is a lemma. For 'hates' the candidates are ['hat', 'hate'], and 'hat' (noun, uz 'shlyapa, do'ppi') matches first. For 'cares' it is ['car', 'care'], and 'car' ('mashina') matches. I checked this against every story token using the shipped lexicon.lep. Real occurrences: S01U09 (A1.1) 'My brother loves music, but he hates football.', where an A1 learner tapping 'hates' is told it means a hat, and S09U04 (C1) '...whether the ministry cares.' This contradicts the method's own contract: 'the reader then shows no gloss rather than a guessed one'.
findings.fix: Try `w.slice(0,-1)` (strip -s) before `w.slice(0,-2)` (strip -es) when the -s form is itself a lemma, i.e. prefer the longest matching stem. Alternatively build an explicit inflection table from the course words list and fall back to [] when more than one stem matches.

findings.title: On native, rebuilding a response that has no X-Request-ID turns its body into the literal text "[object ReadableStream]"
findings.detail: sendWith does `return new Response(response.body, {...})` when the X-Request-ID header is missing (a proxy or CDN answered). On iOS and Android, Expo SDK 57 replaces global fetch with expo/fetch (expo/src/winter/runtime.native.ts:52), whose FetchResponse exposes `.body` as a ReadableStream. The global `Response` constructor is still React Native's whatwg-fetch polyfill. Its `_initBody` has no ReadableStream branch and falls through to `this._bodyText = body = Object.prototype.toString.call(body)` (whatwg-fetch/dist/fetch.umd.js:262). The rebuilt response's body is therefore the string "[object ReadableStream]". For a 2xx, openapi-fetch's JSON.parse throws SyntaxError (shown as client/unknown). For an error, any problem document the proxy sent, such as a 429 with retry_after_s, is lost. Web is unaffected because browser Response accepts streams. Our backend always sets the header, so only responses generated by a proxy go through this path.
findings.fix: Don't rebuild the Response. Return the original and pass the sent requestId alongside it (e.g. a WeakMap<Response, string>, or have problemFromResponse take sentRequestId, as it already can), or rebuild from `await response.arrayBuffer()`.

findings.title: Row and index are two separate writes, so a kill between them leaves an orphaned answer
findings.detail: enqueue does `await setItem(row)` and then `await setItem(index)`. If the process is killed between the two (the native queue can be busy, see the sequential-scan finding), the row exists but is not in the index. It is never listed, synced, exported or deleted by clear(), and nothing reports it. The header comment ('Serialises every write so a crash can never interleave two index updates') covers interleaving but not this window.
findings.fix: Use `AsyncStorage.multiSet([[rowKey,row],[indexKey,index]])`, which runs in one SQLite transaction on native. Or, at start-up, reconcile `getAllKeys()` with the prefix `lep:outbox:<id>:row:` against the index.

findings.title: The packer empties assets/content before validating, so a failed run leaves the app unbuildable
findings.detail: `rmSync(out, { recursive: true, force: true })` runs before the 168-unit, 1,344-node, 37,173-item and 3,019-tier checks. Any `fail()` (lines 43-120) exits with only some u*.lep copied and no index, course, words or lexicon .lep files, while the old src/content/assets.generated.ts still `require`s them, so Metro then fails to resolve the modules. Today's data passes: I re-ran the hash and every u*.lep is byte-identical to the source, with contentVersion sha256:15517a0ea7373e00 matching. This only bites when content is changed.
findings.fix: Validate and write into a temporary directory, then swap it into assets/content (and write the generated .ts files) only after all checks pass.

fe-core.notes:
I read src/api/**, src/outbox/**, src/state/**, src/content/**, src/lib/**, useBootstrap.ts, _layout.tsx and pack-content.mjs, and checked them against the real data, the backend source and the installed library code.

**Solid, verified with evidence:**
- **Zod schemas vs packed data.** I ran schemas.ts (zod 4.6.5, Node type-stripping) over all 168 unit files, index.json and the generated course.lep. Results: 0 unit failures and 0 of 37,173 item failures. Every key present in the data (`p`, `a`, `c`, `fb`, `tg`, `say`, `accepted`, `rejected_with_feedback`, `option_audio`…) is covered, so zod's key stripping drops nothing.
- **Item consistency.** Answer indexes are always in range, pair and bin mappings match their prompts, and order keys are permutations of their options. Only free-response items have empty keys, and the grader handles them as ungraded.
- **Shipped assets.** They are byte-identical to the source, and contentVersion matches a recomputed hash.
- **Memory.** No concern found. Units are 67–114 KB and loaded on demand, lexicon is 1 MB and words 100 KB. The repository's 12-unit cache is effectively superseded by the query cache's 30-minute retention, but real usage stays small.
- **Session refresh.** The single-flight refresh with generation checks around both the response read and the token write is correct for concurrent callers and for sign-out during a refresh. The F2 retry is consistent with the backend's strict reuse detection (app/services/auth.py) and is documented. The backend answers a revoked access token with `invalid_token`, which costs one extra refresh before sign-out, as DECISIONS notes. Reading the JWT `sub` claim to key the learner is sound.
- **Other plumbing.** UUIDv7 bit layout is correct and fits the backend's X-Request-ID pattern. Problem parsing never keeps title or detail. Log redaction covers `lep_rt_` tokens, JWTs, Bearer headers and emails. tokenStorage resolves to memory on web and Keychain/Keystore on native as intended. The backend's CORS settings expose X-Request-ID and Retry-After and allow the client's headers.

**Main risks:**
1. Web blank screen when fonts take more than 12 s to load.
2. Web multi-tab writes overwriting the outbox index and learner progress.
3. Outbox failures that are silent or stick until restart.
4. Sync hard-wired to `null`, contradicting DECISIONS §9.4.
5. No reconnect/foreground refetch on native (no onlineManager/focusManager wiring), which, combined with upkeep being gated on /v1/me, mis-counts ignored reminders.

**Context worth knowing:**
- OUTBOX_CAPACITY (5,000) plus no drain path means active learners will eventually have answers refused by design.
- Android AsyncStorage defaults to a 6 MB database. My estimate for a full outbox is about 4.5–5 MB including SQLite overhead: probably under the limit, but with little margin.

**Out of my slice, not verified:** the screens' own use of these hooks.

findings.title: Registration strips spaces from the start and end of the password, but login does not, so these accounts can never sign in
findings.detail:
`RegisterRequest.model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", str_strip_whitespace=True)` also applies to the `password: SecretStr` field. `LoginForm` has no such setting. I checked this in the venv (pydantic 2.13.5): `RegisterRequest(password="  secret pass word  ", ...)` gives `'secret pass word'`, while `LoginForm(password="  secret pass word  ")` keeps `'  secret pass word  '`. Argon2 hashes the stripped value, and `service.login` later verifies the raw value, which fails with `invalid_credentials`.

The frontend sends the password unchanged on both paths (`lep-frontend/src/app/(auth)/onboarding/account.tsx` L67-69 sends `password`, and `sign-in.tsx` L32 calls `session.signIn(email.trim(), password)`).

Scenario: a learner registers with "my long passphrase " (trailing space, which is common with a password manager, a paste, or a mobile keyboard). Registration returns 201 and the app works until the session ends. After that, every sign-in fails, and with no password-reset flow the account is lost.

A second effect: "          abc" passes the client's 10-character check, but the server strips it to "abc" and answers with a confusing length error.

No test registers and then logs in with a password that has surrounding whitespace.
findings.fix: Stop stripping passwords. Remove `str_strip_whitespace` from the model config and strip `email`, `tz` and `l1` explicitly (for example with `Annotated[str, StringConstraints(strip_whitespace=True)]` on those fields only). Keep `_password_not_email` comparing a stripped copy. Add an integration test that registers with a password that has spaces at the start and end and then logs in with the identical string.

findings.title: Database errors raised during a query (statement timeout, admin shutdown) become 500s and are never retried by Celery
findings.detail:
SQLAlchemy 2.0.54's asyncpg adapter translates query-time errors (`_asyncpg_error_translate`: `asyncpg.exceptions.PostgresError: self.Error`). So `QueryCanceledError` (statement_timeout=5 s), `AdminShutdownError`, deadlocks and similar errors reach the app as plain `sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError`, not as `OperationalError` or the raw asyncpg class.

`is_dependency_failure` only does `isinstance(exc, DEPENDENCY_ERRORS)` plus an OSError check. The asyncpg entries in that tuple (`QueryCanceledError`, `AdminShutdownError`, ...) can therefore never match at query time. I checked in the venv: `DBAPIError.instance('SELECT 1', {...}, AsyncAdapt_asyncpg_dbapi.Error('x'), ...)` gives `<class 'sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError'>`, and `is_dependency_failure(...)` returns False.

Result: a slow query or a PostgreSQL restart mid-query answers 500 `internal_error`, logged as `unhandled_exception`, instead of 503 with Retry-After. The frontend treats 5xx and 503 differently. `app/workers/tasks.py` L48 `autoretry_for=DEPENDENCY_ERRORS` has the same gap, so the purge task does not retry these errors either.

The unit test (`tests/unit/test_errors.py` L287-299) only feeds raw exceptions, never a SQLAlchemy-wrapped one, so it hides this.
findings.fix: In `is_dependency_failure`, unwrap `sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError`: treat it as a dependency failure when `exc.connection_invalidated` is set, or when the SQLSTATE (`getattr(exc.orig, 'sqlstate', None)`, or `exc.orig.__cause__`) is one of 57014 (query_canceled), 57P01/57P02/57P03, 53300, or class 08. Use the same predicate for Celery: drop the tuple-based `autoretry_for` and retry manually when `is_dependency_failure(exc)`. Add tests built from a real wrapped error, for example a `pg_sleep` that runs past a 100 ms statement_timeout.

findings.title: Logs include SQL bind parameters (emails, Argon2 hashes)
findings.detail:
The engines are built without `hide_parameters=True` (`app/db.py` L54-64). The last-resort handler then logs exception text in two places:
- `_log.warning("dependency_unavailable", error_type=..., error=str(exc))` (L167)
- `_log.error("unhandled_exception", exc_info=exc)` (L169), which `dict_tracebacks` renders including the exception string.

For any SQLAlchemy statement error, `str(exc)` contains `[parameters: ...]`. Checked in the venv: `str(DBAPIError.instance('SELECT 1', {'email': 'victim@example.com'}, ...))` prints `[parameters: {'email': 'victim@example.com'}]`.

Scenario: a statement timeout during `LearnerRepository.insert` writes the learner's email and full `$argon2id$...` password hash into the logs. A timeout during login writes the email. `_redact` only checks top-level event keys, so nothing catches it. This contradicts DECISIONS §2.9, which says SQL is kept out of logs because it can contain learner data.
findings.fix: Pass `hide_parameters=True` to both `create_async_engine` calls in `app/db.py` (API and worker), and to the Alembic engine too. In `_classify`, log `error_type` and the SQLSTATE, not `str(exc)`. Add a test asserting that an email used in a failing query never appears in the captured log.

findings.title: A Redis outage makes refresh and logout return 503, so every learner is locked out within 15 minutes
findings.detail:
`limit_refresh_ip` calls `enforce(container.limits.refresh_ip, client_ip(request), fail_open=False)` and is attached to both `/refresh` and `/logout` (`app/api/v1/auth.py` L102 and L118). The rationale in DECISIONS §2.7 ("an outage cannot open the door to password guessing") does not apply here: refresh tokens are 256-bit random values, so there is nothing to guess.

Effect: while Redis is unreachable, the `/v1` traffic fails open, but every refresh gets 503. Access tokens last 900 s, so within one access-token lifetime every signed-in learner loses all authenticated API access (lesson sync, the future outbox ingest) even though PostgreSQL is healthy. The 503 detail also says "Sign-in is briefly unavailable" (`rate_limit.py` L119) for a refresh or logout.

No test covers refresh when Redis is down; `test_rate_limit.py` L77-88 covers login only.
findings.fix: Use `fail_open=True` for refresh and logout, or a small in-process fallback bucket. Keep fail-closed for login and register only. Make the message specific to the endpoint, and add an integration test for refresh with Redis down.

findings.title: The per-account login limit uses Python casefold(), which can disagree with PostgreSQL citext lower(), giving several limit buckets for one account
findings.detail:
Code:
```
email = form.username.strip()
await container.rate_limiter.enforce(container.limits.login_account, email.casefold(), fail_open=False)
```
The account itself is found by `Learner.email == cast(email, CITEXT)`, which compares with the database's `lower()` (libc UTF-8 ctype in the postgres images).

The two disagree for U+0130 'İ': glibc `towlower` maps it to 'i', so `admİn@gmail.com` finds the account `admin@gmail.com`. Python gives `'admİn@gmail.com'.casefold() == 'admi̇n@gmail.com'` (verified), which is a different bucket.

An attacker therefore gets 2^n separate 10-per-15-min buckets against one account, where n is the number of i/I letters in the email. The per-IP limit does not stop this from a botnet. This weakens the main brute-force control described in DECISIONS §2.7. It depends on the database's collation provider, so it is plausible rather than certain.
findings.fix: Key the per-account limit on a form the database cannot disagree with. One option: resolve the account first (`SELECT id ... WHERE email = $1::citext`) and key on learner_id when it exists, falling back to a normalized string. Another: reject login usernames that are not in `email_validator` normalized form after NFKC plus ASCII-only lowercasing.

findings.title: Per-IP limits key on the full IPv6 address, so one client can rotate through its /64
findings.detail: `client_ip()` returns `request.client.host` unchanged, and every IP limit (`ip`, `login_ip`, `register_ip`, `refresh_ip`) hashes that exact string into its key. A single IPv6 subscriber normally controls a /64 or larger (2^64 addresses) and can use a new source address per request. That removes the per-IP login and registration limits completely (mass account creation, credential stuffing across accounts). Only the per-account bucket remains, and see the casefold finding for that one.
findings.fix: Normalize before keying: use `ipaddress.ip_address(host)`, map IPv4-mapped IPv6 to IPv4, and truncate IPv6 to its /64 (or /56) network. Add a unit test.

findings.title: Per-IP limits are too low for shared addresses (carrier CGNAT, school Wi-Fi) and also apply to authenticated traffic
findings.detail:
`router = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(limit_ip)])` applies the 300-per-minute per-IP bucket to every /v1 request, including authenticated ones that already have their own per-account bucket. The defaults are `rate_limit_register_ip_per_hour=20` (refill 1 per 180 s, fail-closed), `rate_limit_refresh_per_minute=30` and `rate_limit_login_ip_per_minute=20` (`config.py` L184-189).

Uzbek mobile operators commonly put many subscribers behind one public IPv4 (CGNAT), and classrooms share one address. Examples:
- 30 students on one Wi-Fi registering together: the 21st gets 429, and the 30th waits about 30 minutes.
- More than about 450 concurrently active learners on one NAT address exhaust the refresh bucket.
- Phase 2+ sync and content endpoints will drain the 300/min `ip` bucket for everyone on that address.
findings.fix: Skip the per-IP `ip` bucket for authenticated requests (the per-account limit covers them), or check the IP limit only when there is no valid principal. Raise the default register and refresh per-IP limits substantially, rely on per-account and per-device limits, and document how to tune them for CGNAT.

findings.title: Strict refresh-token reuse detection plus the frontend's retry-on-lost-response signs learners out on flaky networks
findings.detail:
`if candidate.token_used_at is not None: await repo.revoke(candidate.session_id, reason="refresh_token_reuse", at=now)` revokes the whole session on any replay, even one a second after rotation. The frontend (`lep-frontend/src/api/session.ts` L195-200, F2) retries a refresh whose response was lost with the same token. Whenever the first request reached the server, that retry is guaranteed to hit this branch, revoke the session and sign the learner out.

On mobile networks this will be the most common cause of unexplained sign-outs. DECISIONS R13 records strict reuse detection as an open product ruling, but the two halves now contradict each other: the client comment says the retry 'either succeeds' when it in fact always ends the session.
findings.fix: Decide R13 now. Recommended: a short reuse interval (5–30 s). If the presented token was used within the window, its successor is still unused, and the request comes from the same session, rotate again from the successor and return a new pair instead of revoking. Otherwise remove the client retry (F2) and accept a sign-out on a lost response.

findings.title: The local stack allows only http://localhost:5173, but the Expo web build and e2e run on :8081 and :4173
findings.detail: `LEP_CORS_ORIGINS: http://localhost:5173` in compose and in `.env.example` L34; the backend default is no CORS at all. The frontend README (L35) says the backend 'allows web origins http://localhost:8081 and http://localhost:4173', and `playwright.config.ts` serves on :8081, 'an origin the backend's CORS allows by default'. Neither is true, so the web app and the Playwright e2e suite against `docker compose up` fail CORS preflight on every API call.
findings.fix: Set `LEP_CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:8081,http://localhost:4173` in docker-compose.yml and .env.example, and correct the frontend README/playwright comments so they do not promise a default.

findings.title: An empty LEP_REDIS_PASSWORD (or an empty secret file) passes the production Redis-auth guard
findings.detail: `_require_redis_auth` only checks `password is None`. pydantic-settings turns an empty variable or an empty secret file into `SecretStr('')`. Verified: with LEP_ENV=prod and LEP_REDIS_PASSWORD= set to empty, `load_settings(Settings)` succeeds with `SecretStr('')`. redis-py then sends no AUTH (`if self.credential_provider or (self.username or self.password)`), so production runs against an unauthenticated Redis despite the guard. An empty `LEP_METRICS_TOKEN` likewise produces a token nobody can present.
findings.fix: Add `min_length=1` to the secret fields (`redis_password`, `metrics_token`, `db_password`, `db_migrator_password`), or treat empty values as None and fail in prod.

findings.title: /metrics is unauthenticated unless a token is configured, and production does not require one
findings.detail: `token = container.settings.metrics_token; if token is not None: ...`. If no token is set, anyone who can reach the API can read `auth_events_total` (login failures, reuse detections), per-route traffic and pool state. Unlike the database TLS and Redis password checks, the production validator does not enforce `metrics_token`.
findings.fix: Require `LEP_METRICS_TOKEN` when `env == 'prod'`, or serve metrics on a separate internal port.

findings.title: Any client can force 100% trace sampling with a traceparent header
findings.detail: `sampler=ParentBased(TraceIdRatioBased(settings.otel_sample_ratio))` follows the sampled flag of a remote parent. FastAPIInstrumentor reads `traceparent` from the incoming request, so a client sending `traceparent: 00-<id>-<id>-01` makes every request it sends sampled and exported. That defeats `otel_sample_ratio` (0.05) and inflates collector cost.
findings.fix: Use `ParentBased(root=TraceIdRatioBased(r), remote_parent_sampled=TraceIdRatioBased(r), remote_parent_not_sampled=TraceIdRatioBased(r))`, or drop `traceparent` from untrusted clients at the edge.

findings.title: Registration stores the email-validator normalized email, but login looks up the raw string
findings.detail: `RegisterRequest.email: EmailStr` stores `validate_email(...).normalized`: IDNA domains are decoded to Unicode and text is NFC-normalized. Verified: `user@xn--bcher-kva.example` is stored as `user@bücher.example`. Login does `email = form.username.strip()` with no normalization, so a learner who signs in with exactly the string they registered cannot find their account. The same applies to decomposed (NFD) Unicode local parts typed on some keyboards.
findings.fix: Normalize the login username with the same `email_validator.validate_email(..., check_deliverability=False).normalized`, falling back to the raw string if it is invalid. Add a test.

findings.title: The purge deletes up to 5,000 sessions per statement, with cascades, under the API's 5 s statement timeout
findings.detail: `WorkerSettings` inherits `db_statement_timeout_ms=5_000`. `purge_sessions_before` deletes up to 5,000 sessions in one `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... LIMIT 5000)`, and ON DELETE CASCADE removes each session's retained refresh tokens: one row per rotation, roughly every 15 minutes of use, kept until expiry. At scale this can exceed 5 s. Because of the DBAPIError finding, the resulting QueryCanceledError is not retried. Every day would then fail on the same first batch, so the tables grow without bound. (Plausible at production volume; not reproduced.)
findings.fix: Give the worker its own statement timeout (or `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` in the purge), lower the batch size, and purge a batch's refresh tokens before deleting its sessions. Log progress per batch.

findings.title: The tests miss the failure modes that hide the findings above
findings.detail:
- `test_dependency_failures_are_recognised` only uses synthetic raw exceptions, never a SQLAlchemy-wrapped `DBAPIError`.
- No integration test logs in with a password that had surrounding whitespace at registration.
- No test covers refresh or logout with Redis down.
- `test_passwords_and_tokens_never_reach_the_logs` covers only the happy path, never a failed query.
- `OffsetClock` cannot expire access tokens, because `TokenService.verify_access_token` uses PyJWT's real clock while `issue_access_token` uses the injected clock. Access-token expiry leading to refresh is therefore never integration-tested.
- Integration tests were not run in this audit (no Docker on this machine); the 98 unit tests pass.
findings.fix: Add the specific tests listed in the other findings. Pass the injected clock's time into PyJWT (decode with `verify_exp=False` and check `exp`/`nbf` against `clock.now()`) so expiry can be tested deterministically.

backend.notes:
I read every file under app/, migrations/, tests/, plus docker-compose.yml, Dockerfile, pyproject.toml, deploy/ and DECISIONS.md. The 98 unit tests pass in .venv (python 3.12). Integration tests could not run because Docker is unavailable on this machine.

Overall quality is high. Several things I checked and found correct:
- The refresh-rotation core is sound. `lock_for_refresh` locks the token and session rows `FOR UPDATE OF refresh_tokens, auth_sessions`, so concurrent refreshes are serialized. The reuse branch commits the revocation before raising. The session-revoked check comes before the reuse check. A refresh token's expiry is capped by the absolute session lifetime.
- Revocation is immediate: `authenticate` looks up the session on every request.
- Argon2 runs outside transactions, behind a CapacityLimiter, with a dummy hash so unknown emails take the same time.
- The JWT is pinned on alg, typ (`at+jwt`) and kid.
- Problem+json is used everywhere and never echoes input. The body limit also covers chunked bodies.
- The Lua token bucket uses Redis TIME. Least privilege is enforced by tests. CHECK constraints mirror the API's validation, and a test proves the models and migrations produce the same schema.
- uvicorn 0.53's proxy-header parsing is correct (it takes the right-most untrusted hop).
- Secret files are stripped of trailing newlines.

Confirmed issues, verified in the venv:
- **Password stripped at registration but not at login** (high). Accounts whose password has spaces at the start or end can never sign in again.
- **Query-time database errors** become 500s instead of 503s and are not retried by Celery, because SQLAlchemy wraps them as plain DBAPIError.
- **Logs include SQL bind parameters**, including emails and password hashes.
- **Refresh and logout fail closed** when Redis is down, which locks every learner out within 15 minutes.
- **Rate-limit keys:** the login limit's casefold() disagrees with PostgreSQL's lower() (plausible bypass), raw IPv6 addresses allow rotation, and the per-IP limits are too low for carrier CGNAT.
- **Contract drift with the frontend:**
  - CORS origins: the backend allows 5173, the web app runs on 8081 and 4173.
  - Strict reuse detection (R13) combined with the frontend's F2 retry makes every lost refresh response end in a sign-out.

Patterns new backend code must follow:
1. **DI container.** Process-wide clients live in `AppContainer` (`app/container.py`), built in the lifespan from `Settings`: settings, metrics, clock, engine, sessionmaker, redis, rate_limiter, limits (`RateLimits.from_settings`), hasher, tokens, policy. Handlers get it through `ContainerDep`. Never create clients at import time.
2. **Dependencies (`app/deps.py`).**
   - `DbSession` gives one AsyncSession per request, cached across dependencies (`expire_on_commit=False`, `autoflush=False`).
   - Services are built per request from the container plus the session, following the `get_auth_service` pattern.
   - `CurrentPrincipal` verifies the JWT, checks the session is live, then applies the per-account limit.
   - Every /v1 route inherits `limit_ip` from the router. Extra limits are `Depends(limit_x)` with an explicit `fail_open` choice.
3. **Transactions.** Handlers and services open short explicit `async with session.begin()` blocks. Never hold one across Argon2, HTTP or LLM calls. Repositories never commit.
4. **Repositories (`app/repositories`).** SQLAlchemy Core statements against the ORM tables, returning frozen dataclasses of plain values, with no business rules. Cast citext comparisons to CITEXT. Use `pg_insert(...).on_conflict_do_nothing().returning()` for idempotent inserts.
5. **Domain logic** is pure (`app/domain`, mypy --strict, no I/O). Time comes only from the injected `Clock`. TIMESTAMPTZ everywhere via `type_annotation_map`; ruff DTZ bans naive datetimes. Primary keys are app-generated `uuid7()`.
6. **Errors.** Subclass `AppError` with ClassVar status, type and title; `type` is a stable snake_case slug the clients branch on. Field errors go through `ValidationFailed([FieldError(...)])`. Document responses with `problem_responses(...)`. Regenerate openapi.json with `make openapi`: a unit test fails if it is stale, and the frontend generates its schema from it.
7. **Migrations.** Hand-written revisions named `NNNN_slug`, using the naming convention in `Base.metadata`.
   - Every new table needs an explicit `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ... TO lep_app_rw`. Append-only tables get SELECT and INSERT only, plus raising triggers. There are no default privileges.
   - `updated_at` columns use the `lep_set_updated_at()` trigger, and CHECK constraints mirror the schema validation.
   - `test_schema` must stay green: model/migration parity with compare_type, and a downgrade to base and back.
   - Migrations run with a 5 s lock_timeout and no statement timeout.
   - New tables must also be added to `TABLES` in `tests/integration/conftest.py`, or rows leak between tests.
   - Design conflict to resolve before Phase 4: the planned beat job that creates monthly partitions, and the erasure job, need DDL or DELETE rights the `lep_app` worker role does not have. They need a separate role and settings class.
8. **Configuration.** Add each setting to the right class (`Settings` for the API, `WorkerSettings`, `MigrationSettings`). Secrets are `SecretStr`, readable from /run/secrets. Every setting must be documented in the README (`test_docs` enforces this). Production guards go in `_consistent`.
9. **Celery.** Tasks must be idempotent (acks_late, reject_on_worker_lost), JSON only, declared as `shared_task(name="lep.<area>.<verb>")`, with the async body run via `asyncio.run` on a per-task NullPool engine. Add the module to `TASK_MODULES` and schedules to `beat_schedule`. Retry only on dependency failures, but use a predicate rather than the current tuple (see the DBAPIError finding).
10. **Observability.** Log through structlog `get_logger` with event-style keys; only top-level sensitive keys are redacted. Metrics are labelled by route template. New counters go on `Metrics`.
11. **Tests.** Integration tests use `start_app` and `settings_for` (limits default to `NO_LIMIT`) with `OffsetClock`. Access-token expiry runs on real time.

Open risks to carry into later phases:
- R13 (refresh-token reuse grace window) and R14 (breached-password screening) are still undecided.
- There are no password-reset, account-deletion or export endpoints yet.
- A web client gets no refresh cookie (frontend F8).
- `db_ssl_mode=require` encrypts without verifying the server certificate.
- Production does not require Redis TLS.
